title: The Sum of Sines: the Tailor's Orphan, the Institut d'Egypte, and the Theory of Heat
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Auxerre, birth in the tailor's house
stops.date_confidence: Birth date attested (MacTutor; Wikipedia EN/FR). The exact house is not identified in any source reached; town-centre coordinates serve as the anchor. The parents' deaths are dated only as 'before he was ten'.
stops.campa: Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier is born at Auxerre in Burgundy, the son of a tailor. Both parents are dead before he is ten, and the boy is placed first in a pensionnat kept by the organist Joseph Pallais, then recommended to the Bishop of Auxerre, who finds him a place among the Benedictines. The family has nothing to leave him, and every place he holds from here forward is one that somebody else opens for him. The tailor's house is identified by no source reached: the town keeps its cathedral and its episcopal palace, and no address for him.
suggested_refs: The cathedral quarter of Auxerre and the episcopal palace of the bishop who placed him

stops.name: Auxerre, the Benedictine military school
stops.date_confidence: Year traditional (FR Wikipedia and MacTutor agree on about 1780; no month attested, defaulted to January). The 1783 Bossut prize inside this stop is attested by MacTutor. Coordinates approximate the historic Benedictine quarter; the 1780s campus footprint is unconfirmed.
stops.campa: He enters the Ecole royale militaire of Auxerre, administered by the Benedictines, and reads literature first. At thirteen or fourteen he turns to mathematics, and the direction of his life closes behind him. In 1783 he takes the first prize for a study of Bossut's work on mechanics. The English and French accounts name his earlier schooling differently, the Convent of Saint Mark in one, the pensionnat Pallais in the other, and neither tradition is dropped here. He is an orphan with a prize in mechanics and no rank, in a kingdom that gives commissions by birth.
suggested_refs: Charles Bossut, Traite elementaire de mechanique, the prize subject of 1783

stops.name: Saint-Benoit-sur-Loire, the novice who never takes vows
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (MacTutor; FR Wikipedia); month unknown, defaulted to January. Coordinates corrected: the research pool carried 47.7908 / 2.2911, about 2.5 km off in open country; EN Wikipedia gives 47.8103 / 2.3067 for the commune and abbey.
stops.campa: At nineteen he enters the Benedictine abbey of Saint-Benoit-sur-Loire to train for the priesthood, and teaches mathematics to the younger novices while he waits. He never takes the vows. The dissolution of the religious orders empties the abbey and returns him to the world in 1789, a man of twenty-one with a novice's training, no orders, no property, and a reputation in one small town for algebra. The Loire runs past a basilica whose tower has stood since before the Capetians.
suggested_refs: The basilica of Saint-Benoit-sur-Loire (Fleury Abbey), where he taught the novices

stops.name: Paris, the paper on algebraic equations
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (MacTutor); month and day not established, defaulted to January. Central Paris coordinates used: the Academy sat at the Louvre, but no source reached places the reading in a named room.
stops.campa: He comes up to Paris and reads a paper on the solution of numerical equations before the Academie royale des sciences, work he will return to for the rest of his life and never quite finish. The city he presents it in is months from the fall of the Bastille. He goes home to Auxerre with the manuscript and no post, and the Academy that heard him will be suppressed within four years by the Convention. The completed analysis of equations is published only after his death.
suggested_refs: Fourier's posthumous Analyse des equations determinees, the work begun with this 1789 paper

stops.name: Auxerre, teaching where he was taught
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (MacTutor); month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He is made a teacher at the Ecole royale militaire of Auxerre, the school that took him in as an orphan, and stands where his own masters stood. He teaches mathematics, and whatever else the school needs; the Benedictines who ran it are being dispersed around him by the same decrees that emptied the abbey. For four years he stays in the town of his birth while France remakes itself from the ground, and then the politics of the town come to find him.
suggested_refs: The dissolution decrees of 1790 and their effect on the Benedictine teaching houses

segments.name: The Terror, the Committee, and the Two Arrests

stops.name: Auxerre, a seat on the Revolutionary Committee
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (MacTutor, quoting Fourier's own letter); month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He takes a seat on the Revolutionary Committee of his district and speaks at the popular society, defending men before it and making the enemies a provincial committee makes. He writes of what he expects from the Republic in a sentence that will be quoted against the rest of his life. The Terror is not yet a word he uses. Within a year this committee work will put him in a cell, and within two the men who put him there will be dead. He is twenty-five and believes the Revolution can be argued with.
stops.quote: the sublime hope of establishing among us a free government
stops.quote_source: Fourier's own letter of 1793, quoted in MacTutor (St Andrews), 'Joseph Fourier'
suggested_refs: The records of the popular society of Auxerre, 1793

stops.name: Auxerre, arrest under the Terror
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor gives only July 1794; the day 4 July comes from the encyclopedia tradition (Wikipedia EN/FR). Contradiction of precision rather than substance, left open. The prison building at Auxerre is not named in any source reached.
stops.campa: He is arrested in the summer of the Terror on charges connected with the affair at Orleans, where he had spoken in defence of local men, and imprisoned. He expects the guillotine and says so. In Paris on the ninth of Thermidor Robespierre goes to the scaffold himself, and the machinery reverses; Fourier is let out. He walks into a France that has just decided, for reasons having nothing to do with him, to stop killing. The prison he was held in is not named by any source that survives to be read.
suggested_refs: The Orleans deputation affair of 1794 and the charges laid against its defenders

stops.name: Paris, the Ecole normale de l'an III
stops.date_confidence: Opening date attested (Wikipedia FR: 20 January 1795; the school closes 19 May 1795). MacTutor confirms Fourier's nomination and attendance and names Lagrange, Laplace, and Monge as teachers.
stops.campa: Nominated to the newly founded Ecole normale, he sits in the amphitheatre of the Museum d'histoire naturelle at the Jardin des Plantes and hears Lagrange, Laplace, and Monge. He is a provincial schoolmaster of twenty-six lately out of a cell. The school lasts four months and closes in May, and in that time the men teaching it learn his name. Lagrange gives up a chair to him within two years. Lagrange and Laplace sit on the committee that refuses his heat memoir twelve years later, and Monge is on the ship that takes him to Egypt.
suggested_refs: The published Seances des Ecoles normales, transcripts of the l'an III lectures

stops.name: Paris, the second arrest
stops.date_confidence: Date from Wikipedia FR. MacTutor states plainly that sources disagree about the cause of his release; the disagreement is preserved rather than resolved. Place of detention not named in any source reached; central Paris coordinates used as placeholder.
stops.campa: He is arrested a second time, in Paris, in the counter-swing that follows Thermidor, and imprisoned again. He is freed. Beyond that the sources part company: one tradition credits the pleas of his own pupils, another the intervention of Lagrange and Monge, another simply a further shift in the political weather. The disagreement is left standing here. Twice in thirteen months the Revolution has taken him, and twice let him go. The charge that put him inside the second time is not stated in any source reached.
suggested_refs: The Thermidorian arrests of the spring of 1795 and the petitions filed against them

stops.name: Paris, the school at the Palais Bourbon
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (MacTutor); month not established and set to September to preserve sequence after the June arrest. Coordinates are the school's seat 1794-1804 near the Palais Bourbon; the move to the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève is dated 1804 by Wikipedia FR, correcting the 1805 given in the research pool.
stops.campa: He begins teaching at the College de France and is appointed to the Ecole centrale des travaux publics, on the Palais Bourbon side of the river, the school about to be renamed Ecole polytechnique. He teaches analysis and mechanics to the first classes of an institution invented to supply the Republic with engineers. The school will move across to the Montagne Sainte-Genevieve in 1804, after his time in it. For two years he teaches in Paris and is not arrested, which nothing in the previous ten years had allowed him to count on.
suggested_refs: The Hotel de Lassay and Palais Bourbon buildings, first seat of the Ecole polytechnique

stops.name: Paris, Lagrange's chair
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (MacTutor; Wikipedia); the exact date within 1797 is not established and is defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Lagrange gives up the chair of analysis and mechanics at the Ecole polytechnique, and Fourier is appointed to succeed him. Two years earlier he had been sitting in Lagrange's audience at the Ecole normale, newly out of a cell. He is twenty-nine and holds the most exacting mathematical teaching post in France, in a school whose graduates will run the armies, the bridges, and the mines of an empire not yet declared. He has one year in the chair before a general with a fleet comes to the Institute asking for men who can be spared.
suggested_refs: The Ecole polytechnique registers of professors, 1794-1798

segments.name: The Fleet, the Delta, and the Institut

stops.name: Toulon, embarkation for a destination not announced
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia FR). Coordinates inherited byte-identical from pierre_francois_bouchard.journey.json, which records the same embarkation at 43.1242 / 5.928.
stops.campa: He embarks at Toulon in the fleet Bonaparte has assembled for a destination the government has not announced, attached to the expedition as a scientific adviser among the corps of savants: mathematicians, chemists, engineers, draughtsmen, orientalists. Monge is aboard. So is a young engineer officer named Pierre-Francois Bouchard, whose own road to Egypt begins at the same quay. Nobody in the convoy outside Bonaparte's cabin knows whether they sail for Ireland, for Sicily, or for Egypt.
suggested_refs: The muster rolls of the Commission des sciences et des arts, Toulon, May 1798

stops.name: Valletta, the Knights give up the island
stops.date_confidence: The fleet's occupation of Malta on 10 June 1798 is attested (MacTutor; Wikipedia EN). Fourier's presence ashore is inferred from his passage with the convoy and is not attested for him by name.
stops.campa: The fleet takes Malta from the Knights of Saint John on the way, and the savants look out at a fortress island that has been a religious order's state for two and a half centuries and ceases to be one inside a week. Bonaparte reorganizes the island's government in six days and sails on, leaving behind a garrison that will be besieged for two years. Whether Fourier goes ashore is nowhere recorded; he is on the ships that anchor here, and that is all the sources will support.
suggested_refs: The Grand Harbour of Valletta and the surrender of the Order of Saint John, June 1798
sources: Wikipedia EN, 'French campaign in Egypt and Syria'

stops.name: Marabout, the landing west of Alexandria
stops.date_confidence: Landing near Marabout 1 July 1798, city taken 2 July (Wikipedia EN, 'French campaign in Egypt and Syria'). The research pool's claim that Alexandria fell on 1 July conflated the two, and its preserved '28 June' infobox contradiction no longer exists in the article; both hedges dropped.
stops.campa: The army lands on the beach at Marabout, west of Alexandria, and takes the city the following day. The savants come ashore behind the infantry into a heat none of them has prepared for, and the Commission des sciences et des arts begins its work in a port it has just helped to conquer. Bouchard lands with the same fleet. Napoleon, whose own journey crosses this coast on the same date, is already on the road inland before the instruments are unloaded.
suggested_refs: The beach at Marabout and the Alexandria landings of 1 July 1798
sources: Wikipedia EN, 'French campaign in Egypt and Syria'

stops.name: Imbaba, the Pyramids and the road to Cairo
stops.date_confidence: Battle date attested (Wikipedia EN). Fourier's presence at the battle itself is not separately attested; his attachment to the travelling savant corps is the basis for the stop. French entry into Cairo 22-24 July, folded into this stop.
stops.campa: At Imbaba across the river from the pyramids the Mamluk cavalry breaks on the French squares, and the road to Cairo opens. The scientific commission travels with the army's train. Within three days the French are in Cairo, and the mathematicians and engineers are quartered in the palaces of a beaten government and told to survey, measure, and describe. Napoleon's own journey records the same march into the same city. The savants have a country to inventory and, as they are about to learn, no way home.
suggested_refs: The Description de l'Egypte plates of Giza and Imbaba, drawn from this advance
sources: Wikipedia EN, 'French campaign in Egypt and Syria'

stops.name: Aboukir Bay, the fleet burned
stops.date_confidence: Date attested (MacTutor). Coordinates supplied by the writer for Aboukir Bay: the research pool carried no lat/lng for this event.
stops.campa: Nelson finds the French fleet at anchor in Aboukir Bay and destroys it in a night action, and the expedition ceases to be an expedition. The army that took Egypt in three weeks cannot leave it. For the savants the disaster is the making of their work: cut off from France, with no prospect of recall and nothing else to do, they will spend three years measuring, drawing, and copying a country no European scholarly body has ever had at its disposal. The Description de l'Egypte is a by-product of a naval defeat.
suggested_refs: The wreck of L'Orient in Aboukir Bay, 1 August 1798

stops.name: Cairo, the founding of the Institut d'Egypte
stops.date_confidence: Foundation 22 August 1798 at the palace of Hassan Kashif, first session 23 August, attested by Wikipedia FR, 'Institut d'Egypte'. Correction carried out: Costaz was secretaire-adjoint, assistant secretary, not a co-equal named alongside Fourier as the research pool had it.
stops.campa: The Institut d'Egypte is founded in the palace of Hassan Kashif outside Cairo and holds its first session on the twenty-third of August: Monge president, Bonaparte vice-president, Fourier secretary, Louis Costaz assistant secretary. Twelve men sit in the mathematics division, Bonaparte among them. They are ordered to study the useful arts of Egypt, to answer the government's questions, and to publish. Fourier keeps the secretaryship for the whole of the occupation, and every memoir the Institut produces crosses his desk.
suggested_refs: The minutes of the Institut d'Egypte, first session, 23 August 1798

stops.name: Cairo, charge of the memoirs
stops.date_confidence: November 1798 given by the research pool from Wikipedia EN, 'Description de l'Egypte'; MacTutor dates the collating charge across 1798-1801 without a starting month. Fontanes's remark is reported by Arago, who does not date it.
stops.campa: He is given charge of collating the reports of the Institut's sections, the antiquities and the canals and the natural history and the mirages, into one body of work for eventual publication. It is an editor's commission handed to a mathematician, and out of it comes the Description de l'Egypte, the publication the expedition is remembered by. He writes its Historical Preface himself, and the preface is read in Paris as a piece of literature before anyone there has seen a single plate.
stops.quote: This introduction was published under the title of Historical Preface: Fontanes saw in it the graces of Athens and the wisdom of Egypt united together.
stops.quote_source: Francois Arago, 'Joseph Fourier,' in Biographies of Distinguished Scientific Men, trans. Smyth, Powell and Grant (London, 1857)
suggested_refs: Fourier's Preface historique to the Description de l'Egypte

stops.name: Aswan, the first cataract
stops.date_confidence: Year only; month unknown, defaulted to January. Wikipedia FR attests Fourier's Upper Egypt exploration with Louis Costaz in general terms; this specific site is a reconstructed stop on that documented itinerary, not attested for him by name. The same reservation covers Philae (24.0247, 32.8841), named in the campa.
stops.campa: The commission pushes south into Upper Egypt with Louis Costaz, and Fourier goes with it as far as the first cataract at Aswan, where the Nile breaks over granite and the boats must be hauled. The island temple of Philae stands just upstream, its colonnades still up to the roofline. What the survey sees here it draws, and what it draws becomes plates. His presence at each particular site along this river is a reconstruction from a documented itinerary rather than an itinerary of his own that anyone wrote down.
suggested_refs: The Philae plates of the Description de l'Egypte, Antiquites vol. I
sources: Description de l'Egypte, documented Upper Egypt itinerary

stops.name: Dendera, the ceiling of the zodiac
stops.date_confidence: Year only; month unknown, defaulted to January. Reconstructed from the Description's documented Upper Egypt itinerary; Fourier's individual presence at Dendera is not separately attested.
stops.campa: At Dendera the survey enters the temple of Hathor and finds in a roof chapel a circular zodiac, the sky carved as a disc held up by figures. The draughtsmen copy it, and the plate becomes one of the most argued-over images in the Description, because the arrangement of the constellations looks as though it dates the ceiling, and the date it appears to give is older than the chronology Europe reads out of its Bible. The commission's presence here is attested. Fourier's own is not, and is not claimed.
suggested_refs: The Dendera zodiac plate in the Description de l'Egypte and the chronology controversy it opened
sources: Description de l'Egypte, documented Upper Egypt itinerary

stops.name: Rosetta, the stone comes out of the wall
stops.date_confidence: Date and coordinates inherited byte-identical from pierre_francois_bouchard.journey.json. That Fourier examined the stone personally is stated by no source reached and is recorded as a gap; he is placed here only as the officer of the institution that received the find.
stops.campa: At Fort Julien near Rosetta an engineer officer supervising repairs to a wall pulls out a black slab carrying the same decree in three scripts. Pierre-Francois Bouchard sends word up to Cairo, where the Institut of which Fourier is permanent secretary takes the find in hand, has it copied, and prints impressions for Europe. No source reached here says that Fourier ever looked at the stone himself, and the silence is left as a silence. He is the man whose signature is on the institution that receives it.
suggested_refs: Fort Julien at Rosetta and the Institut's inked impressions of the trilingual decree

stops.name: Cairo, the oration for Kleber
stops.date_confidence: Kleber was assassinated at Cairo on 14 June 1800; the date used here is the assassination, since the date of Fourier's funeral oration is not established in the sources reached. The oration text is printed by Arago.
stops.campa: General Kleber, left in command of an army the First Consul has abandoned, is assassinated in his garden at Cairo, and Fourier delivers the funeral oration before the army and the Institut. It is the performance of a man who has spent two years administering an occupation and knows exactly who is listening. Bonaparte will later read the word illustrious applied to Kleber in Fourier's Historical Preface, remark that someone has directed his attention to the epithet, and then let it stand.
stops.quote: Ah! how many of you would have aspired to the honour of throwing yourselves between Kleber and his assassin! I call you to witness, intrepid cavalry, who rushed to save him upon the heights of Koraim, and dispelled in an instant the multitude of enemies who had surrounded him!
stops.quote_source: Joseph Fourier, funeral oration for General Kleber, Cairo, quoted in Francois Arago, 'Joseph Fourier' (1857 trans.)
suggested_refs: The garden of the Ezbekieh palace at Cairo, where Kleber was killed on 14 June 1800

stops.name: Cairo, the garrison capitulates
stops.date_confidence: The Cairo garrison capitulated under Belliard in June 1801 and was evacuated under terms (Wikipedia EN). Exact day not fixed in the sources reached, defaulted to the first. Fourier is placed here for the corps and not by name; one strand of the tradition instead attaches him to the Alexandria capitulation two months later.
stops.campa: The Cairo garrison capitulates to the British and Ottoman armies, and the terms allow the French to be evacuated rather than held. The savants leave with the garrison, carrying their notes. Three years of measurement go aboard as paper. Where Fourier stands during these weeks is documented for the corps and not for the man: the sources place the Commission in the June evacuation and do not name him inside it, and another strand of the tradition puts him at Alexandria in September instead.
suggested_refs: The Cairo capitulation of June 1801 and the evacuation terms granted to the Commission
sources: Wikipedia EN, 'French campaign in Egypt and Syria'

stops.name: Alexandria, the last capitulation
stops.date_confidence: Menou's capitulation at Alexandria is attested for 2 September 1801. Correction carried out: the research pool placed Fourier among the evacuated here and tied his return to Menou; MacTutor never mentions Menou, and the Cairo savants had sailed in June. His presence at this surrender is not attested. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from pierre_francois_bouchard.journey.json.
stops.campa: Menou signs the capitulation of Alexandria and the French occupation of Egypt ends. Whether Fourier is still in the country to see it is doubtful: the savants attached to the Cairo garrison had sailed in June, and no source reached here names him at this surrender. The stop is kept as the closing of the campaign that made him, and marked as a place he was probably no longer standing in. He goes home with three years of another country in his baggage and a secretaryship behind him.
suggested_refs: The Alexandria capitulation of 2 September 1801 and the disposition of the Commission's collections
sources: Wikipedia EN, 'French campaign in Egypt and Syria'

stops.name: Toulon, the uncertain return
stops.date_confidence: The year is contradicted between sources: MacTutor and Wikipedia EN say 1801, Wikipedia FR says 1802. Left standing; the later date is used for ordering only. The port of landing is named by nobody reached; Toulon, the port of departure, is used as a placeholder pin.
stops.campa: He comes back to France, and the sources cannot agree on when. The English accounts say 1801 and the French say 1802, and the port he stepped ashore at is named by nobody. Toulon serves as the pin because Toulon is where he sailed from. He is thirty-three or thirty-four, has published nothing of consequence, and resumes his professorship at the Ecole polytechnique expecting to spend the rest of his life as a mathematician in Paris. He will not hold the chair for long.
suggested_refs: The returning transports of the Commission des sciences et des arts, 1801-1802

stops.name: Grenoble, appointed prefect of the Isere
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia FR: 'Le 12 fevrier 1802, Napoleon le nomme prefet de l'Isere.' MacTutor and Wikipedia EN loosely date the appointment to 1801, and the research pool carried both; the documented date is used and the older tradition noted. Term ends 1815, not 1814 as the pool had it.
stops.campa: Napoleon names him prefect of the Isere, and he goes to Grenoble to govern a department at the foot of the Alps. The appointment is a reward and a removal at once: the Consul keeps his savants where they are useful and out of the capital. Fourier holds the prefecture for thirteen years, and writes the theory of heat in the hours the administration leaves him. The book that comes out of those hours is printed in 1822, twenty years after he first reports to Grenoble.
stops.quote: "Do not," said he, "submit half measures to me. You have to pronounce judgment upon high personages: we must either cut off their heads or invite them to dinner."
stops.quote_source: Napoleon Bonaparte to Fourier, quoted in Francois Arago, 'Joseph Fourier' (1857 trans.)
suggested_refs: The prefecture of the Isere and its administrative registers, 1802-1815

stops.name: Grenoble, the boy Champollion at the prefect's house
stops.date_confidence: Champollion reached Grenoble 27 March 1801 and was born 23 December 1790, so he was ten and not eleven at any such meeting; the research pool's 'eleven-year-old' is corrected. Sources date the visit c. 1801 or c. 1802; March 1802 is used for ordering. Wikipedia EN flags the anecdote's truth as uncertain.
stops.campa: A boy from Figeac, living in Grenoble with his elder brother, is brought to the prefect's house and shown a collection of Egyptian antiquities and papyri. Told that the writing on them cannot be read, the child is said to have answered that he would be the one to read it. The encyclopedia that carries the story flags its truth as uncertain, and it is carried here as tradition. The alliance behind it is not in doubt: Fourier becomes Champollion's protector and keeps him at his table for years.
suggested_refs: Fourier's private collection of Egyptian antiquities at Grenoble

stops.name: Bourgoin, the marshes drained
stops.date_confidence: No single date: the works run the length of the prefecture, 1802-1815. MacTutor gives 'draining the swamps of Bourgoin' verbatim. The road is contradicted: MacTutor sends it to Turin, Wikipedia FR to Briancon by the col du Lautaret. The pool's 'Mont Cenis' detail was unsourced and is struck.
stops.campa: The prefect drains the marshes of Bourgoin, reclaiming farmland from standing water that has bred fever in the Isere lowlands for as long as there has been a village on them. He also drives a new road out of Grenoble through the mountains, and the sources disagree about which one: one account sends it over the Alps to Turin, the other up to Briancon by the col du Lautaret. The disagreement is left open. He governs the department for thirteen years and is remembered in it for water and for roads.
suggested_refs: The Bourgoin marsh drainage works and the Napoleonic alpine road programme

stops.name: Grenoble, heat in solid bodies
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor: 'His work on the topic began around 1804.' The research pool's geography lens gave 1802-1807 and is corrected to 1804-1807. Month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: At Grenoble he begins the work on the propagation of heat in solid bodies, in the hours the prefecture leaves him. He arrives at a partial differential equation governing the flow, and then at the harder problem of solving it for a body whose boundaries are held at fixed temperatures. The answer he reaches is an infinite series of sines, which he claims will represent any function whatever, continuous or broken. It is the claim the best analysts in Europe will refuse to accept from him.
stops.quote: PRIMARY causes are unknown to us; but are subject to simple and constant laws, which may be discovered by observation, the study of them being the object of natural philosophy.
stops.quote_source: Joseph Fourier, The Analytical Theory of Heat, Preliminary Discourse, trans. Alexander Freeman (Cambridge University Press, 1878)
suggested_refs: Fourier's 1807 manuscript memoir, Sur la propagation de la chaleur dans les corps solides

stops.name: Paris, the memoir read at the Institute
stops.date_confidence: Reading date attested to the day (MacTutor). The Lagrange and Laplace objection is dated 1808 by MacTutor and is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of December the memoir on the propagation of heat in solid bodies is read at the Institute, and a committee is named to examine it: Lagrange, Laplace, Monge, Lacroix, the same men who taught him in the amphitheatre at the Jardin des Plantes. Lagrange and Laplace object to the trigonometric series, and Lagrange never withdraws the objection. The memoir is not published. Fourier goes back to Grenoble and to the prefecture carrying the refusal of the two men whose approval he wanted most.
stops.quote: There cannot be a language more universal and more simple, more free from errors and from obscurities, that is to say more worthy to express the invariable relations of natural things.
stops.quote_source: Joseph Fourier, The Analytical Theory of Heat, Preliminary Discourse, trans. Alexander Freeman (Cambridge University Press, 1878)
suggested_refs: The Institute committee report of 1807-1808 on Fourier's heat memoir

stops.name: Grenoble, the Hotel de Lesdiguieres and the Imperial Faculty
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by Wikipedia FR ('Il cree en 1810 la Faculte (universite) Imperiale de Grenoble, dont il devient le recteur'); month unknown, defaulted to January. Correction carried out: the research pool called it an 'Imperial Academy of Grenoble', which is not the institution's name.
stops.campa: He founds the Imperial Faculty of Grenoble and becomes its rector, and holds evening gatherings at the Hotel de Lesdiguieres where Champollion, now a professor of history at twenty, sits at his table talking about hieroglyphs. The prefect who once showed a boy his antiquities now keeps that boy out of the army. Arago, writing the eulogy twenty years later, counts the exemption among the services Fourier rendered to science, and names the device used: the title of pupil of the School of Oriental Languages, which Champollion had held at Paris.
stops.quote: I cannot refrain from alluding to the service which Fourier rendered to science by retaining Champollion. The young professor of history of the Faculty of Letters of Grenoble had just attained the twentieth year of his age. Fate calls him to shoulder the musket. Fourier exempts him by investing him with the title of pupil of the School of Oriental Languages which he had borne at Paris.
stops.quote_source: Francois Arago, 'Joseph Fourier,' in Biographies of Distinguished Scientific Men, trans. Smyth, Powell and Grant (London, 1857)
suggested_refs: The Hotel de Lesdiguieres at Grenoble, seat of the prefecture and of Fourier's evenings

stops.name: Golfe-Juan, the Emperor comes ashore
stops.date_confidence: Date and coordinates inherited byte-identical from napoleon.journey.json, which records the Elba landing and the march north through the mountains toward Grenoble. That file does not record Fourier's response to the approach; the gap is filled here from Fourier's own sources.
stops.campa: Napoleon comes ashore from Elba at Golfe-Juan with a thousand men and strikes north through the mountains, and the road he takes leads to Grenoble, where Fourier has been prefect for thirteen years. The prefect has spent the winter trying to organize opposition to exactly this. He has a few days to decide whether to receive the Emperor who made him, or to be found in the city when the Emperor walks into it.
suggested_refs: The route Napoleon, from Golfe-Juan through the Alpine passes to Grenoble, March 1815

stops.name: Grenoble, the prefect leaves before the Emperor arrives
stops.date_confidence: Month attested (Wikipedia FR: March 1815); day not established and defaulted to the first, which places this stop alongside the Golfe-Juan landing rather than after it. MacTutor confirms the attempted opposition and the flight.
stops.campa: With the column coming up the valley, Fourier leaves Grenoble by one road as Napoleon's soldiers come in by another. The city opens its gates. It is the second time in his life that a change of regime finds him on the wrong side of it, and the second time he survives the finding. Napoleon, told the prefect has fled, does not have him arrested; within weeks the two are reconciled and Fourier is handed another department. The Empire has ninety days left to run.
suggested_refs: The gates of Grenoble, opened to Napoleon on 7 March 1815

stops.name: Lyon, prefect of the Rhone
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (Wikipedia FR); the date of appointment is given by no source reached and is set to April for ordering between the March flight and the 17 May removal. That removal date is itself attested.
stops.campa: Napoleon makes him prefect of the Rhone at Lyon during the Hundred Days, the second city of France and the one most likely to decide the southeast. He holds it for a matter of weeks. No source reached here gives the date he took it up, nor the reason he was taken out of it; the removal alone is dated, the seventeenth of May, a month before Waterloo. He is dismissed by the Empire and not by the Bourbons, and nobody troubles to write down why. Lyon is the last administrative office he ever holds.
suggested_refs: The Rhone prefecture registers for the Hundred Days

stops.name: Paris, dismissed and pensioned on paper
stops.date_confidence: Removal from the prefecture attested to the day (Wikipedia FR). The pension of 6000 francs granted 10 June 1815 and never received is attested by MacTutor and folded into this stop.
stops.campa: Removed from the prefecture on the seventeenth of May, he goes to Paris with no office and no income. On the tenth of June the Emperor grants him a pension of six thousand francs. Eight days later the Empire ends at Waterloo, and the pension is never paid. He is forty-seven: twice a prefect, once a professor, author of an unpublished memoir that two of the greatest mathematicians in France have rejected, and a client of a patron who is being shipped to the South Atlantic.
suggested_refs: The imperial pension decree of 10 June 1815, unpaid

stops.name: Paris, the Bureau of Statistics of the Seine
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (Wikipedia EN); month not established, set to June to preserve sequence after the 17 May dismissal. Exact address of the bureau not established in the sources reached; central Paris coordinates used as placeholder.
stops.campa: He is named director of the Bureau of Statistics of the Seine, and the post restores him an income and a footing in the capital. The bureau counts births, deaths, grain, and rents. He does the work, and goes on with the heat in the same rooms. Twenty years after the amphitheatre at the Jardin des Plantes he is back in Paris with a salary and a manuscript, and the manuscript is the one Lagrange refused. The rest of his life is spent making the Academy take it.
suggested_refs: The statistical returns of the department of the Seine, 1815-1822

stops.name: Paris, elected to the Academie des sciences
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (MacTutor; Wikipedia FR); month and day not established, defaulted to January. Wikipedia FR records that an earlier admission had been blocked on political grounds.
stops.campa: He is elected to the Academie des sciences at the Palais de l'Institut on the Quai Conti. An earlier election had been blocked on political grounds, the government refusing to confirm a man who had served Napoleon twice and taken a prefecture from him during the Hundred Days. The second attempt carries. He is forty-nine. The men who examined his heat memoir in 1807 are now his colleagues, and their objection to the trigonometric series is still standing on the record.
suggested_refs: The Palais de l'Institut on the Quai Conti, seat of the Academie des sciences

stops.name: Paris, permanent secretary and the Theorie analytique
stops.date_confidence: Both the election to the permanent secretaryship on Delambre's death and the publication by Firmin Didot fall in 1822 (MacTutor; Wikipedia EN); neither is dated to the month in the sources reached, so both are set to January and combined in one stop.
stops.campa: Delambre dies and Fourier is elected permanent secretary of the mathematical section, the office that runs the Academy's business and its printing. In the same year the Theorie analytique de la chaleur comes off Firmin Didot's presses, the printing arranged by Delambre before his death. Fifteen years after Lagrange refused it, the book appears with the sines intact. A Glasgow boy named William Thomson will read it at sixteen and take from it the mathematics with which he weighs the age of the Earth.
stops.quote: Profound study of nature is the most fertile source of mathematical discoveries. Not only has this study, in offering a determinate object to investigation, the advantage of excluding vague questions and calculations without issue; it is besides a sure method of forming analysis itself, and of discovering the elements which it concerns us to know, and which natural science ought always to preserve.
stops.quote_source: Joseph Fourier, The Analytical Theory of Heat, Preliminary Discourse, trans. Alexander Freeman (Cambridge University Press, 1878)
suggested_refs: The 1822 Firmin Didot first edition of the Theorie analytique de la chaleur

stops.name: Paris, the memoir on the temperature of the globe
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (Wikipedia EN, 'Greenhouse effect'); month not established, defaulted to January. Pouillet's strengthening of the argument is dated 1827 and 1838; Ekholm's coinage of the term to 1901.
stops.campa: He publishes an argument about the temperature of the globe: that the atmosphere holds the sun's heat in a way that leaves the Earth's surface warmer than direct radiation alone would leave it. Pouillet strengthens the case in 1827 and again in 1838. The phenomenon goes without a name for another seventy-seven years, until Nils Gustaf Ekholm calls it the greenhouse effect in 1901. The man who wrote that heat penetrates every substance in the universe applies the sentence to the planet he is standing on.
stops.quote: Heat, like gravity, penetrates every substance of the universe, its rays occupy all parts of space. The object of our work is to set forth the mathematical laws which this element obeys. The theory of heat will hereafter form one of the most important branches of general physics.
stops.quote_source: Joseph Fourier, The Analytical Theory of Heat, Preliminary Discourse, trans. Alexander Freeman (Cambridge University Press, 1878)
suggested_refs: Fourier's 1824 memoir on the temperatures of the terrestrial globe and the planetary spaces

stops.name: Paris, the fall on the stairs
stops.date_confidence: Date attested (Arago, verbatim; Wikipedia EN). Coordinates are those of his residence in the old rue d'Enfer, an approximate match to a street later absorbed into Boulevard Saint-Michel and rue Henri-Barbusse.
stops.campa: He has had attacks of an aneurism of the heart since Egypt, and in Paris the suffocations come often enough that nobody mistakes the cause. On the fourth of May he falls down a flight of stairs, and the fall drives the disease past anything that had been feared for him. The tradition adds that he kept his rooms overheated and himself heavily wrapped, a habit traced back to the Nile; that detail is repeated everywhere and confirmed by none of the sources reached here.
stops.quote: Fourier had already experienced, in Egypt and Grenoble, some attacks of aneurism of the heart. At Paris, it was impossible to be mistaken with respect to the primary cause of the frequent suffocations which he experienced. A fall, however, which he sustained on the 4th of May, 1830, while descending a flight of stairs, aggravated the malady to an extent beyond what could have been ever feared.
stops.quote_source: Francois Arago, 'Joseph Fourier,' in Biographies of Distinguished Scientific Men, trans. Smyth, Powell and Grant (London, 1857)
suggested_refs: Arago's eloge of Fourier, read before the Academie des sciences

stops.name: Paris, death at 19 rue d'Enfer
stops.date_confidence: Date and address attested (Wikipedia FR). Coordinates approximate: rue d'Enfer no longer exists under that name, having been absorbed into Boulevard Saint-Michel and rue Henri-Barbusse.
stops.campa: He dies on the sixteenth of May at his residence, 19 rue d'Enfer, in his sixty-third year. The street will later be swallowed by the Boulevard Saint-Michel and the rue Henri-Barbusse and will cease to exist under that name. He leaves the Theorie analytique published, the Historical Preface to the Description printed, and the analysis of numerical equations unfinished on the table. He has been permanent secretary of the Academy for eight years, and holds the office until the day he dies. His last words, as Arago sets them down, are a call for vinegar.
stops.quote: "Quick, quick! some vinegar! I am fainting!"
stops.quote_source: Joseph Fourier's last words, 16 May 1830, quoted in Francois Arago, 'Joseph Fourier' (1857 trans.)
suggested_refs: The site of 19 rue d'Enfer, now within the Boulevard Saint-Michel quarter

segments.name: The Egyptian Tomb and the Series

stops.name: Pere Lachaise, the Egyptian tomb
stops.date_confidence: Burial in Division 18 under a monument with Egyptian motifs is attested (Wikipedia EN for the motifs, FR for the division); the burial day is not given, so the month is used. Coordinate discrepancy inside the research pool, flagged not averaged: the afterlife lens gives 48.8614 / 2.3931, the geography lens 48.8606 / 2.3928. The tomb inscription was not recovered.
stops.campa: He is buried in the eighteenth division of Pere Lachaise under a monument cut with Egyptian motifs, three years on the Nile put into stone over a man whose work is a theory of heat. Six weeks after the funeral, Jacobi writes to Legendre from Konigsberg that Fourier held the object of mathematics to be public utility and the explanation of natural phenomena, and that a philosopher should have known better. The argument about what mathematics is for opens over this grave.
stops.quote: It is true that M. Fourier had the opinion that the principal aim of mathematics was public utility and explanation of natural phenomena; but a philosopher like him should have known that the sole end of science is the honor of the human mind, and that under this title a question about numbers is worth as much as a question about the system of the world.
stops.quote_source: C. G. J. Jacobi to Legendre, Konigsberg, 2 July 1830; English rendering as given in MacTutor (after N. Rose, Mathematical Maxims and Minims, 1988). French original verified in Jacobi, Gesammelte Werke Bd. I, pp. 454-455
suggested_refs: The Fourier monument, Division 18, Pere Lachaise, Paris

stops.name: Auxerre, the statue melted down
stops.date_confidence: Erection in 1849 and destruction in a wartime metal drive are given by Wikipedia FR, which does not specify the year of the melting; the erection year is used and the month defaulted to January. Whether the 2012 subscription produced a new statue is not established by any source reached.
stops.campa: Auxerre raises a bronze statue of its tailor's orphan in 1849. The Occupation takes it down and melts it in one of the metal drives of the Second World War, and the town puts up a simple medallion in its place to mark the affront. In 2012 the science and technology centre of Burgundy opens a national subscription for a replacement; whether one now stands in Auxerre is not established by any source reached here. Nor is the year the bronze went into the furnace: the account that records the melting does not date it.
suggested_refs: The 1849 Fourier monument at Auxerre and the medallion that replaced it

stops.name: Paris, the name on the Eiffel Tower
stops.date_confidence: The 72 names were added at the tower's completion in 1889; no month applies, defaulted to January. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the interlock lens and rene_hauy.journey.json (48.8583, 2.2945); the afterlife lens of the research pool gives 48.8584, and the divergence is recorded rather than resolved.
stops.campa: His name is cut into the frieze under the first balcony of the Eiffel Tower, one of seventy-two engineers and scientists gilded around the four faces. Lavoisier is there, and Poisson, and Dulong, and Rene Hauy, another name gilded around the same iron. The frieze puts him among the men the Republic wanted read from the ground, a hundred years to the season after the abbey emptied and sent a novice with no orders and no property back into the world.
suggested_refs: The frieze of 72 names beneath the first balcony of the Eiffel Tower

stops.name: Grenoble, the university that took his name
stops.date_confidence: The merger into Universite Grenoble Alpes is dated 2015 by Wikipedia FR; the month is not relevant and is defaulted to January. The lunar crater Fourier was adopted by the IAU in 1935, and the Fermi anecdote is drawn from fermi.journey.json, where it is a mathematical inheritance and not a shared place.
stops.campa: The science university of Grenoble carries the name Universite Joseph Fourier until a 2015 merger folds it into Universite Grenoble Alpes; streets in Grenoble, Auxerre, Chartres, and Saint-Martin-de-Crau keep it, and a crater near the Mare Humorum has been Fourier since 1935. The transform built on his series is the ordinary instrument of signal processing, spectroscopy, and quantum mechanics. Enrico Fermi, sitting an entrance examination at Pisa, solves a vibrating rod by Fourier analysis and is admitted.
suggested_refs: Universite Joseph Fourier, Grenoble, 1970-2015; the lunar crater Fourier, Mare Humorum
